label: Goryeo Korea
pitch:
Goryeo gave Korea the name the world still uses. Founded by a maritime lord who bound 29 warlord clans by marriage, it built a Confucian bureaucratic state, repelled three Khitan invasions, perfected jade-green inlaid celadon, and carved the most complete Buddhist canon on Earth — 81,258 woodblocks that survive today.

🔑 Key Facts:
• Seo Hui talked the northern border to the Yalu River in 993 without a battle, then Gang Gam-chan annihilated a 100,000-man Khitan army at Gwiju in 1019
• A 1170 military coup reduced kings to puppets; the Choe house then ran a hereditary military dictatorship for 60 years
• The court resisted the Mongols from Ganghwa Island for nearly 30 years before becoming a Yuan 'son-in-law nation'
• The Jikji was printed with movable metal type in 1377 — 78 years before Gutenberg

🤔 Why It Matters: Goryeo forged the bureaucratic-aristocratic, Buddhist, and finally Neo-Confucian foundations that the 500-year Joseon dynasty inherited — and survived the single most destructive invasion in Korean history with its civilization's memory intact.

🎲 Wild Card: General Yi Seong-gye was ordered to invade Ming China in 1388; he marched to the border, turned his whole army around, seized the government, and four years later founded the dynasty that ruled Korea until 1910.

spans.label: Founding & Unification
spans.description: Wang Geon, a maritime lord of Songak, overthrew the tyrant Gung Ye in 918, outlasted Later Baekje, and peacefully absorbed a dying Silla in 935 — reunifying the peninsula under Goryeo by 936.

spans.label: The Bureaucratic State & the Khitan Wars
spans.description: Gwangjong and Seongjong forged a Confucian bureaucratic monarchy out of a confederation of warlords, while three Khitan (Liao) invasions were turned back by diplomacy and the crushing victory at Gwiju.

spans.label: The Aristocratic Golden Age
spans.description: An age of inlaid celadon, world trade, and the Samguk Sagi — rotting from within through the Yi Ja-gyeom coup, Myocheong's revolt, and the festering contempt for the military officer class.

spans.label: The Military Rule Era
spans.description: The 1170 coup massacred the civil officials and reduced kings to puppets; the Choe house ran a hereditary military dictatorship through private armies, even as it resisted the Mongols from Ganghwa Island.

spans.label: The Son-in-Law Nation
spans.description: A century as a Mongol in-law state: Yuan princess-queens, 'Chung-' kings raised at Dadu, forced fleets against Japan, and the channel through which Neo-Confucianism entered Korea.

spans.label: Reform, Collapse & the Birth of Joseon
spans.description: Gongmin's anti-Yuan reforms and Sin Don's land revolution unraveled; Red Turbans and pirates battered the realm; Yi Seong-gye turned his army around at Wihwa Island and founded Joseon in 1392.

events.label: Gyeon Hwon Founds Later Baekje
events.description: A peasant-born general, Gyeon Hwon, carved a kingdom out of Silla's collapsing southwest, reviving the name of the long-dead Baekje state and opening the Later Three Kingdoms war.

events.label: Gung Ye Proclaims Later Goguryeo
events.description: A one-eyed ex-monk and former bandit, Gung Ye, declared himself king of a northern state he called Later Goguryeo (later Taebong), claiming to be the future Buddha Maitreya.

events.label: Wang Geon Founds Goryeo
events.description: Gung Ye's paranoid tyranny pushed his own generals to revolt; they enthroned the maritime lord Wang Geon, who took the reign name Taejo and named his kingdom Goryeo — a deliberate claim on the glory of ancient Goguryeo.

events.label: The Capital Moves to Kaesong
events.description: Taejo moved his capital from Gung Ye's Cheorwon to his own power base of Songak, renamed Gaegyeong (modern Kaesong) — a merchant city that would anchor the dynasty for 470 years.

events.label: Pyongyang Rebuilt as the Western Capital
events.description: Taejo resettled and fortified the ruined city of Pyongyang as a 'Western Capital,' the springboard for a lifelong policy of northward expansion toward the old Goguryeo lands.

events.label: Balhae Falls; Refugees Flood South
events.description: The Khitan destroyed Balhae, the Manchurian successor to Goguryeo. Taejo welcomed tens of thousands of Balhae refugees — including the crown prince — treating their kingdom's fall as a wound to be avenged.

events.label: Disaster at the Battle of Gongsan
events.description: Gyeon Hwon's Later Baekje army ambushed Taejo near Daegu; Goryeo's general Sin Sung-gyeom died wearing the king's armor as a decoy so Taejo could escape — the dynasty's near-death moment.

events.label: Turning Point at the Battle of Gochang
events.description: Goryeo's victory at Gochang (Andong) broke the deadlock with Later Baekje and brought a wave of regional warlords over to Taejo's side.

events.label: Silla Surrenders Peacefully
events.description: The last Silla king, Gyeongsun, judged resistance hopeless and handed his thousand-year kingdom to Goryeo intact. Taejo married into the Silla royal house and treated its aristocracy with conspicuous honor.

events.label: Gyeon Hwon Defects to His Enemy
events.description: Deposed and imprisoned by his own son Singeom, the aged founder of Later Baekje escaped and submitted to Taejo — then guided the campaign that destroyed the kingdom he had built.

events.label: Unification: the Battle of Iljiwon
events.description: At Iljiwon (Seonsan) Goryeo annihilated Later Baekje's army, reuniting the Korean peninsula under one ruler for the first time since Silla's decline.

events.label: Stipend Land Binds the Warlords
events.description: Taejo granted 'merit land' (yeokbunjeon) to the warlords and officers who had backed him, converting a coalition of armed magnates into a landed founding aristocracy — and storing up trouble for his heirs.

events.label: Taejo's Ten Injunctions
events.description: On his deathbed Taejo left ten political-religious commandments to his successors: revere Buddhism but limit the monasteries, distrust the southwest, study the Chinese classics but keep Korean ways — a constitution in miniature.

events.label: The Marriage-Alliance Web
events.description: Taejo took 29 wives from powerful clans across the peninsula, fathering 25 sons and 9 daughters. The web bound the kingdom together — and guaranteed a generation of murderous succession disputes.

events.label: Wanggyu's Rebellion
events.description: The first fruit of the marriage web: the magnate Wanggyu, grandfather of two princes, plotted to seize the throne amid the chaotic reigns of Taejo's first two short-lived successors.

events.label: Gwangjong Takes the Throne
events.description: Taejo's son Gwangjong, watching his brothers die in coup and counter-coup, resolved to break the founding aristocracy's grip and rule as an autocrat on the Chinese model.

events.label: The Slave Review Act
events.description: Gwangjong's Slave Review Act freed people the warlords had illegally enslaved during the wars — restoring them to taxpaying commoner status and gutting the magnates' private manpower at a stroke.

events.label: The Civil Service Examination Begins
events.description: On the advice of the Later Zhou defector Ssang Gi, Gwangjong instituted the gwageo examination: office by tested knowledge of the Confucian classics rather than by birth — the spine of the Korean state for a thousand years.

events.label: Gwangjong Proclaims Himself Emperor
events.description: Gwangjong adopted an imperial title, his own era names, and color-graded official robes, styling Kaesong an 'Imperial Capital' — Goryeo behaving as a self-contained celestial empire.

events.label: The Purge of the Merit Subjects
events.description: Behind the reforms came terror: Gwangjong executed or exiled much of the founding warlord class on charges of treason, a bloodbath that left the throne supreme but the elite traumatized.

events.label: The Jeonsigwa Land System
events.description: Gyeongjong's Jeonsigwa system tied land-revenue rights to bureaucratic rank rather than to birth, financing the new officialdom — though hereditary loopholes would slowly hollow it out.

events.label: Choe Seungno's 28-Point Memorial
events.description: The scholar Choe Seungno handed King Seongjong a sweeping critique of the previous reigns and a blueprint for Confucian government: a founding document of the Korean bureaucratic state.

events.label: The Twelve Mok Provinces
events.description: Seongjong planted twelve provincial governors (mok) across the realm, the first time the central state reached past the capital region into the countryside in a permanent, salaried way.

events.label: The Gukjagam National Academy
events.description: Seongjong founded the Gukjagam, the state Confucian university that trained the scholar-officials who would sit the gwageo and run the ministries.

events.label: Korea's First Coinage
events.description: Seongjong minted iron 'geonwon jungbo' coins, an early and largely unsuccessful attempt to monetize an economy that kept running on rice and cloth for centuries.

events.label: The Three Chancelleries and Six Ministries
events.description: Goryeo adapted the Tang–Song central government — chancelleries to deliberate and draft, six ministries to execute — but bent it around a hereditary aristocratic council, a distinctly Korean hybrid.

events.label: Gangjo's Coup
events.description: The general Gangjo deposed and killed King Mokjong and enthroned Hyeonjong — a regicide the Khitan emperor would seize on as the pretext for invasion.

events.label: The Thousand-Li Wall
events.description: After the Khitan wars Goryeo built a stone rampart across the northern frontier from the Yalu's mouth to the east coast — a 600-mile border wall sealing the won-back north.

events.label: Munjong's Golden Age Opens
events.description: The long reign of Munjong — orderly, prosperous, culturally radiant — became the benchmark by which Goryeo measured every later age of decline.

events.label: The Jeonsigwa Revised Again
events.description: Repeated re-issues of the land-rank system show the state fighting a losing battle against aristocratic families converting revenue grants into permanent private estates.

events.label: The First Khitan Invasion
events.description: The Liao general Xiao Sunning crossed the Yalu with a vast army, demanding Goryeo abandon its Song alliance and submit to the Khitan empire.

events.label: Seo Hui Talks the Border to the Yalu
events.description: Instead of fighting, the envoy Seo Hui out-argued Xiao Sunning face to face — conceding nominal submission while extracting Khitan recognition of Goryeo's right to the lands up to the Yalu River.

events.label: The Six Garrison Settlements
events.description: Goryeo fortified the Gangdong Six Stations east of the Yalu, converting Seo Hui's diplomacy into a permanent, walled northern frontier.

events.label: The Second Khitan Invasion
events.description: The Liao emperor Shengzong personally led 400,000 men, sacked Kaesong, and burned the palace; King Hyeonjong fled to the far south at Naju before a negotiated Khitan withdrawal.

events.label: The First Tripitaka Koreana Begun
events.description: Believing the Buddha would shield the kingdom, Hyeonjong vowed and began carving the entire Buddhist canon onto woodblocks — a state act of faith against the Khitan terror.

events.label: The Third Khitan Invasion
events.description: Liao sent 100,000 troops under Xiao Baeya to punish Goryeo's failure to deliver on its submission; this time Goryeo was ready.

events.label: Gang Gam-chan's Victory at Gwiju
events.description: The 71-year-old scholar-general Gang Gam-chan trapped the retreating Khitan army at Gwiju and annihilated it — barely a few thousand of 100,000 escaped. The Khitan never invaded again.

events.label: A Century of Peace
events.description: After Gwiju, Goryeo balanced formal tribute to Liao against deep trade and cultural ties to Song, buying a hundred years of security through triangular diplomacy.

events.label: Arab Merchants at Kaesong
events.description: Arab and Persian traders ('Daesik') are recorded reaching the Goryeo court with mercury, spices, and ivory — the encounters through which the name 'Korea' entered the wider world's vocabulary.

events.label: The Heungwangsa Temple Complex
events.description: Munjong poured state wealth into vast monasteries such as Heungwangsa near the capital — the fusion of royal power and Buddhist spectacle that the Ten Injunctions had warned against.

events.label: The First Tripitaka Completed
events.description: Seventy-six years of carving produced the first complete Korean Buddhist canon — a triumph of organization that also proved Goryeo could mobilize a kingdom for a single project.

events.label: Uicheon Returns from Song
events.description: A royal prince turned monk, Uicheon, came home from study in Song China with thousands of texts and a mission to heal Korean Buddhism's bitter doctrinal feuds.

events.label: The Cheontae School Founded
events.description: Uicheon established the Cheontae (Tiantai) school to reconcile Korea's scripture-focused and meditation-focused Buddhist traditions — a unification that did not outlive him.

events.label: The Haedong Tongbo Coinage
events.description: Another minting push under Sukjong issued 'Haedong tongbo' coins and even silver 'eunbyeong' vases as currency — used mostly by the state and merchants, ignored by the rice-and-cloth countryside.

events.label: Yun Gwan's Jurchen Campaign
events.description: General Yun Gwan led a special 'Extraordinary Military Corps' north against the rising Jurchen, building Nine Forts in the northeast — then abandoning them within two years as indefensible.

events.label: The Jurchen Found the Jin Empire
events.description: The Jurchen tribes Goryeo had despised as 'barbarians' founded the Jin empire, crushed Liao, and by 1126 forced Goryeo to acknowledge Jin overlordship — a humiliation the elite swallowed.

events.label: A Song Envoy Describes Goryeo
events.description: Xu Jing's illustrated report on his embassy to Kaesong gives a vivid outsider's portrait of Goryeo's wealth, ritual, and the celadon he admired as 'the first under heaven.'

events.label: Yi Ja-gyeom's Coup
events.description: The in-law magnate Yi Ja-gyeom, whose daughters had married the king, tried to seize the throne outright; the fighting burned the palace and exposed how rotten aristocratic government had become.

events.label: Myocheong's Rebellion
events.description: The geomancer-monk Myocheong urged moving the capital to Pyongyang, declaring an empire, and attacking Jin; rebuffed, he revolted, and the kingdom split over its own identity.

events.label: Kim Bu-sik Crushes the Revolt
events.description: The Confucian statesman-historian Kim Bu-sik led the year-long siege that destroyed Myocheong's Pyongyang regime — a victory of the cautious, Silla-rooted, pro-Jin establishment.

events.label: The Samguk Sagi
events.description: Kim Bu-sik compiled the Samguk Sagi, the oldest surviving Korean history — invaluable, and pointedly Silla-centered and Confucian in a way that shaped how Koreans saw their own past.

events.label: The Celadon Apex
events.description: Twelfth-century kilns perfected sanggam inlaid celadon — designs incised and filled with white and black slip under a jade-green glaze — the most prized luxury good in East Asia.

events.label: Goryeo Paper, the World's Finest
events.description: Goryeo's mulberry-bark paper (hanji) was so durable and lustrous that Song China imported it as the best paper on Earth — a craft refined to a technology and a major export.

events.label: The Sky Watchers
events.description: Goryeo's astronomical bureau kept systematic records of eclipses, comets, and sunspots; the dense observational logs preserved in the later Goryeosa remain useful to astronomers today.

events.label: Uijong's Pleasure Pavilions
events.description: King Uijong lavished the treasury on gardens, pavilions, and Buddhist festivals while military officers, barred from honor and pay, stood guard in the rain — the spark drying out.

events.label: The Military Coup of 1170
events.description: At a royal outing, officers led by Jeong Jung-bu massacred the civil officials, deposed Uijong, and seized the state — ending two centuries of civilian aristocratic rule.

events.label: Kim Bo-dang's Failed Restoration
events.description: A loyalist counter-coup to restore Uijong collapsed; the deposed king was murdered, his spine reportedly broken — proof the soldiers would not give power back.

events.label: Jo Wi-chong's Pyongyang Revolt
events.description: A general in the Western Capital rose against the junta; the multi-year war to crush him showed the new regime's authority reached only as far as its armies.

events.label: Gyeong Dae-seung and the Dobang
events.description: The strongman Gyeong Dae-seung built the Dobang, a private bodyguard corps that became the real seat of power — government by household army, the template for what followed.

events.label: The Rise of Yi Ui-min
events.description: A butcher's son risen through the army, Yi Ui-min, clawed to the top of the junta — vivid evidence that in military-rule Goryeo, low birth was no longer a ceiling.

events.label: Choe Chungheon Seizes Power
events.description: Choe Chungheon killed Yi Ui-min and ended the chaotic strongman churn, founding a stable hereditary military dictatorship that would rule Goryeo for sixty years behind puppet kings.

events.label: Manjeok's Slave Uprising
events.description: A palace slave named Manjeok plotted a slave revolt in the capital itself, arguing that since low-born men now ruled, 'are generals and ministers born to their rank?' — betrayed and drowned before it began.

events.label: The Age of Peasant Revolt
events.description: Famine, exploitation, and the collapse of legitimate authority set off a decade of regional risings — Gyeongju, Unmun, Jinju — that the junta drowned in blood.

events.label: The Gyojeong Dogam
events.description: Choe Chungheon ruled not as king but through the Gyojeong Dogam, a personal control agency that taxed, policed, and appointed — the dynasty's real government for half a century.

events.label: The Choe Dictatorship Becomes Hereditary
events.description: Choe Chungheon died and power passed smoothly to his son Choe U — a private military house now inherited the state as if it were an estate.

events.label: First Contact with the Mongols
events.description: Goryeo and a Mongol army cooperated to wipe out Khitan remnants who had fled into Korea — and the Mongols presented the bill: crushing annual 'tribute' and overbearing envoys.

events.label: The Murder That Meant War
events.description: The Mongol envoy Jegüü was killed on the border under murky circumstances; the Mongols broke relations and, six years later, came back as an invading army.

events.label: The First Mongol Invasion
events.description: Ögedei's general Sartai poured into Goryeo, smashing through the north; the court bought a withdrawal with tribute and Mongol overseers it had no intention of obeying.

events.label: The Court Flees to Ganghwa Island
events.description: Choe U moved the king, court, and capital to Ganghwa, a tidal island the Mongol cavalry could not reach — committing Goryeo to decades of resistance while the mainland burned.

events.label: Sartai Killed at Cheoin
events.description: During the second invasion the Mongol commander Sartai was shot dead by the monk Kim Yun-hu and a band of peasants and slaves at a small fortress south of the capital — and the Mongols withdrew again.

events.label: The Original Tripitaka Burns
events.description: Mongol troops burned the woodblocks of the first Tripitaka Koreana, destroying seventy years of work and, to Goryeo eyes, defiling the kingdom's spiritual shield.

events.label: The First Metal-Type Printing
events.description: The court text Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun was printed on Ganghwa with cast-metal movable type — the earliest documented use of the technology anywhere, two centuries before Gutenberg.

events.label: The Tripitaka Koreana Re-Carved
events.description: On Ganghwa, Goryeo vowed and began carving the canon again — 81,258 woodblocks completed by 1251, the world's most complete and accurate Buddhist canon, surviving today at Haeinsa.

events.label: Emergency Remedies of Folk Medicine
events.description: Compiled on besieged Ganghwa, the Hyangyak Gugeupbang catalogued native Korean herbal cures — the oldest surviving Korean medical text, born of a kingdom cut off from Chinese drugs by war.

events.label: Hwangnyongsa Pagoda Destroyed
events.description: The Mongols burned the nine-story wooden pagoda of Hwangnyongsa at Gyeongju, the tallest structure in East Asia and a 600-year-old symbol of Korean Buddhist civilization.

events.label: The Catastrophe of 1254
events.description: In a single campaign Mongol forces took over 200,000 captives and left the countryside, in the chronicle's words, ash and bone — the human cost of the island court's defiance.

events.label: The Choe Dictatorship Falls
events.description: After sixty years, the last Choe dictator was assassinated by his own subordinates; with the war faction broken, Goryeo could finally sue for peace.

events.label: The Crown Prince Meets Kublai
events.description: Goryeo's heir submitted in person — and chose to back Kublai in the Mongol succession war. Kublai won, and remembered: Goryeo would be a privileged vassal, not an erased one.

events.label: The Court Returns to the Mainland
events.description: King Wonjong abandoned Ganghwa and returned the capital to Kaesong, formally ending a century of military rule and a generation of island resistance.

events.label: The Sambyeolcho Rebellion
events.description: The elite Sambyeolcho patrol corps refused to surrender, enthroned their own king, and fought on from Ganghwa to Jindo to Jeju before Goryeo–Mongol forces annihilated them in 1273.

events.label: The Son-in-Law Nation Begins
events.description: King Chungnyeol married a daughter of Kublai Khan; for a century Goryeo kings would be Yuan imperial sons-in-law, raised at the Mongol court and reigning by Mongol leave.

events.label: The First Invasion of Japan
events.description: Forced to build the fleet and supply the troops, Goryeo carried the first Mongol invasion of Japan to Hakata Bay, where a storm wrecked the armada — a ruinous, involuntary war.

events.label: The Field Branch for Japan
events.description: The Yuan planted a 'Branch Secretariat for the Eastern Expedition' (Jeongdong Haengseong) in Goryeo — a permanent organ of Mongol oversight that long outlived the Japan campaigns.

events.label: The Second Invasion and the Kamikaze
events.description: A second, larger fleet sailed against Japan with Goryeo ships and men; a typhoon — the 'divine wind' — destroyed it, drowning tens of thousands and gutting Goryeo's coast and treasury.

events.label: The Ssangseong Commandery
events.description: The northeast around Hwaju was carved off and ruled directly by the Yuan through the Ssangseong Commandery — a hundred-year amputation of Korean territory.

events.label: Tamna Becomes a Mongol Horse Pasture
events.description: Jeju Island (Tamna) was placed under direct Mongol administration as an imperial horse ranch — herds, herders, and a Mongol stamp on the island that outlasted the dynasty.

events.label: Iryeon Compiles the Samguk Yusa
events.description: Under Mongol domination the monk Iryeon gathered the myths, Buddhist tales, and the Dangun foundation legend into the Samguk Yusa — a defiant assertion of a distinct Korean origin.

events.label: Yi Seung-hyu's Jewang Ungi
events.description: The poet Yi Seung-hyu set Korean history in verse, again starting from Dangun — another scholar answering subjugation with a story of ancient, independent Korean nationhood.

events.label: An Hyang Brings Neo-Confucianism
events.description: Returning from the Yuan capital, the scholar An Hyang introduced Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism to Goryeo — the intellectual bomb that would, a century on, blow up the dynasty itself.

events.label: Chungseon's Reform Attempt
events.description: King Chungseon tried to curb the great estates and the in-law cliques; checkmated by Yuan and aristocracy alike, he withdrew to Dadu — a pattern of stillborn reform that would repeat.

events.label: The Manggwondang Academy in Dadu
events.description: Chungseon endowed the Manggwondang study hall in the Yuan capital, where Goryeo and Chinese scholars met — a hothouse that sent Neo-Confucian ideas streaming back to Korea.

events.label: The Tribute of Bodies
events.description: Beyond gold, ginseng, and falcons, the Yuan demanded 'tribute women' and eunuchs; some rose to power in Dadu, but the gongnyeo levies were a generational trauma the chronicles record with shame.

events.label: Gongmin Takes the Throne
events.description: Raised a hostage at the crumbling Yuan court, King Gongmin returned determined to break the Mongol grip while the empire that imposed it was visibly dying.

events.label: Gongmin's Anti-Yuan Revolution
events.description: Gongmin purged the pro-Yuan Gi clan, abolished the Mongol oversight organs, and sent armies to retake the Ssangseong Commandery — recovering the lost northeast in a single bold year.

events.label: The House of Yi Joins Goryeo
events.description: Reclaiming the northeast won Gongmin the allegiance of the frontier warlord Yi Ja-chun and his son Yi Seong-gye — the family that would end the dynasty.

events.label: The Red Turbans Invade
events.description: Chinese Red Turban rebels, smashed by the Yuan, spilled into Korea; in 1361 they sacked Kaesong itself and Gongmin fled south to Andong before Goryeo's generals retook the capital.

events.label: Sin Don's Rise
events.description: Grief-stricken by his queen's death, Gongmin handed reform to the low-born monk Sin Don, an outsider with no clan estates to protect and nothing to lose.

events.label: The Land and Slave Reform
events.description: Sin Don's Directorate of Land and Slaves returned seized estates to their owners and illegally bound people to freedom — wildly popular below, and a death sentence among the aristocracy he robbed.

events.label: Gongmin Assassinated
events.description: Sin Don was purged in 1371 and Gongmin murdered in 1374 by his own attendants; reform from the top had failed, and the dynasty's last chance died with the king.

events.label: Choe Yeong Beats Back the Pirates
events.description: Japanese wokou pirates raided ever deeper, even threatening the capital; the incorruptible old general Choe Yeong's victory at Hongsan made him the dynasty's sword and conscience.

events.label: The Jikji: Movable Metal Type
events.description: Monks at Heungdeoksa in Cheongju printed the Jikji with movable metal type — the oldest such book that survives, produced 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.

events.label: Choe Mu-seon's Gunpowder Bureau
events.description: After prying the gunpowder formula from a Chinese trader, Choe Mu-seon got the court to found a Firearms Directorate — Korea's first cannon, built to kill pirates.

events.label: Cannon at Jinpo, Slaughter at Hwangsan
events.description: Choe Mu-seon's cannon burned the wokou fleet at Jinpo; the pirates stranded ashore were destroyed by Yi Seong-gye at Hwangsan — the victory that made him a national hero.

events.label: The Wihwa Island Turnaround
events.description: Ordered to invade Ming-held Liaodong, Yi Seong-gye marched to the Yalu, judged the war suicidal, turned his army around, seized the capital, and made himself the power behind the throne.

events.label: The Gwajeon Land Law
events.description: Yi Seong-gye and the radical Neo-Confucians burned the old land registers and redistributed revenue rights — destroying the aristocracy's economic base and funding the regime that would replace it.

events.label: Jeong Mong-ju Murdered; Joseon Founded
events.description: When the loyalist scholar Jeong Mong-ju refused to abandon Goryeo, Yi Seong-gye's son had him clubbed to death on Seonjuk Bridge; months later Yi Seong-gye took the throne as Taejo of Joseon.

events.label: Jeong Do-jeon and the New Order
events.description: The revolutionary Neo-Confucian Jeong Do-jeon, who had argued a dynasty losing the people's trust forfeits the right to rule, became the architect of the Joseon state — Goryeo's afterlife was its replacement.
